title: Families and release models
summary: Debian, Red Hat, SUSE, Arch and Alpine families, and LTS, point and rolling releases.

steps.title: The family tree
body: Most distros descend from a few roots. Learn the roots and you know the tools for the whole branch:
| **Debian** | Debian, Ubuntu, Linux Mint, Pop!_OS, Raspberry Pi OS, Kali | `.deb`, `apt` / `dpkg` |
| **Red Hat** | RHEL, Fedora, CentOS Stream, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux, Amazon Linux | `.rpm`, `dnf` (older: `yum`) / `rpm` |
Fedora is upstream of CentOS Stream, which is upstream of RHEL; Rocky and Alma rebuild RHEL-compatible releases. Amazon Linux 2023 is based on Fedora.

steps.prompt: Match the distro to its package tool.

steps.title: Release models
body: | **LTS / point release** | a numbered release every 1-3 years; versions frozen; security fixes backported for 5-10 years; minor point releases (`12.7`, `9.4`) roll up fixes | Ubuntu LTS (`24.04`, every two years, 5 years standard + more with Pro), Debian stable, RHEL, Rocky, Alma, SLES |
| **Regular (short-lived)** | a release every ~6 months, supported for about a year | Fedora, Ubuntu interim releases (`24.10`) |
| **Rolling** | no versions: you update continuously and always have the latest | Arch, openSUSE Tumbleweed, Alpine `edge`, Gentoo |
| **Stream** | a rolling preview of the next point release | CentOS Stream |
Ubuntu version numbers are the year and month: `24.04` is April 2024. Even years with `.04` are LTS.

steps.prompt: You run a payroll server that must keep working for 5 years with minimal changes. Which release model fits?
options: LTS: frozen versions with backported security fixes
steps.explain: Rolling releases change behaviour under you; 6-month releases force an upgrade every year.

steps.prompt: What does this print? (Ubuntu LTS releases are the `.04` releases of even years.)

steps.title: Find the LTS and rolling machines in a fleet
prompt: An inventory job copied `/etc/os-release` from every server into `~/fleet/HOST/os-release`. Answer with `grep` (and
friends), one host name per line, sorted:
1. `~/answers/ubuntu-lts.txt`: the Ubuntu hosts on an **LTS** release. Ubuntu writes `LTS` into `VERSION` (and `PRETTY_NAME`).
2. `~/answers/ubuntu-interim.txt`: the Ubuntu hosts on an **interim** (9-month) release.
3. `~/answers/rolling.txt`: hosts with **no** `VERSION_ID` at all: rolling releases have no version number.

checks.name: ubuntu-lts.txt
checks.cmd: diff ~/answers/ubuntu-lts.txt <(grep -l "^ID=ubuntu" ~/fleet/*/os-release | xargs grep -l "LTS" | xargs -n1 dirname | xargs -n1 basename | sort)
checks.fail: The LTS list does not match. Find the files with `ID=ubuntu`, then keep those whose `VERSION` says `LTS`. Write host names (the folder names), not paths.

checks.name: ubuntu-interim.txt
checks.cmd: diff ~/answers/ubuntu-interim.txt <(grep -l "^ID=ubuntu" ~/fleet/*/os-release | xargs grep -L "LTS" | xargs -n1 dirname | xargs -n1 basename | sort)
checks.fail: The interim list does not match: Ubuntu hosts whose `VERSION` has no `LTS`. `grep -L` lists files that do **not** match.

checks.name: rolling.txt
checks.cmd: diff ~/answers/rolling.txt <(grep -L "^VERSION_ID=" ~/fleet/*/os-release | xargs -n1 dirname | xargs -n1 basename | sort)
checks.fail: The rolling list does not match: hosts whose `os-release` has no `VERSION_ID=` line.

hints: `grep -l PATTERN files` prints the names of files that match; `grep -L` the ones that do not. `grep -l '^ID=ubuntu' ~/fleet/*/os-release`.
Chain them: `grep -l '^ID=ubuntu' ~/fleet/*/os-release | xargs grep -l LTS`. Turn `/home/learner/fleet/web-01/os-release` into `web-01` with `awk -F/ '{print $(NF-1)}'`.
solution: grep -l '^ID=ubuntu' ~/fleet/*/os-release | xargs grep -l LTS | awk -F/ '{print $(NF-1)}' | sort > ~/answers/ubuntu-lts.txt
grep -l '^ID=ubuntu' ~/fleet/*/os-release | xargs grep -L LTS | awk -F/ '{print $(NF-1)}' | sort > ~/answers/ubuntu-interim.txt
explain: Ubuntu LTS releases come every two years in April (22.04, 24.04, 26.04) with 5 years of standard support; interim
releases (25.10) get 9 months, so a server on one is a ticket waiting to happen. Rolling distributions (Arch) have no
